title: Melioidosis, a Deadly Soil Infection That Mimics TB, Is Going Undetected Across India
excerpt: A 15-centre Lancet study found the infection in 8.9% of high-risk hospital patients, and one in five died. The disease is not notifiable in India, labs routinely misidentify the bacterium, and standard TB treatment does not work against it.
body:
• A study in The Lancet Global Health screened 2,953 high-risk hospital patients at 15 Indian tertiary centres between January 2023 and December 2025 and found culture-confirmed melioidosis in 262 of them — 8.9%. Fifty of those patients, 19.1%, died in hospital.
  • Melioidosis is caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei, a bacterium that lives in soil and surface water. It mimics tuberculosis, pneumonia and sepsis, and only a laboratory culture can confirm it.
  • Diabetes is the strongest risk factor. If a family member with diabetes in coastal or monsoon-drenched India has a fever, cough or foot ulcer that does not improve on standard treatment, ask the treating doctor specifically whether melioidosis has been ruled out by culture.
  • The disease is not notifiable in India and appears on no national or state disease list, so there is still no official count of how many people it infects or kills.

A 48-year-old man with uncontrolled diabetes arrived at hospital with a swollen lower limb, high fever and breathlessness. A sample from his ankle joint was first identified as a different bacterium altogether, and changes in his lungs pointed his doctors towards tuberculosis. Only when cultures of his blood and joint pus were examined closely did the real cause emerge: Burkholderia pseudomallei, the soil bacterium that causes melioidosis. His blood cultures cleared around the 21st day of the correct treatment, and he recovered, Atish Mohapatra of the Kalinga Institute of Medical Sciences in Bhubaneswar recounts in The Hindu.

His case is not an outlier. It is the pattern.

One in Eleven High-Risk Patients

The largest Indian picture so far comes from a study published in The Lancet Global Health, led by Nitin Gupta of Kasturba Medical College, Manipal. Researchers assessed high-risk hospitalised adults at 15 tertiary-care centres between January 2023 and December 2025. Of 2,953 patients, 262 — 8.9% — had culture-confirmed melioidosis, and 50 of them died in hospital, a mortality rate of 19.1%.

Global modelling paints a far larger hidden burden: an estimated 165,000 cases and about 89,000 deaths a year worldwide, most of them never diagnosed. In India, doctors who work on the disease say reported cases cluster in Odisha, coastal Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, coastal Karnataka, Kerala, Goa and Maharashtra, with a growing number in Assam and the Northeast and in West Bengal. The map, they stress, reflects where laboratories know how to look — not necessarily where the bacterium lives.

"Two decades ago, the disease was virtually unknown in India — often undiagnosed or misdiagnosed as tuberculosis, sepsis of unknown origin or other tropical bacterial infections."

— Chiranjay Mukhopadhyay, Kasturba Medical College, Manipal

Built to Be Missed

Melioidosis can produce fever, cough, chest pain, skin ulcers, joint infections, abscesses in the liver, spleen, prostate or brain, and full-blown sepsis — a range so wide that clinicians call it a great mimicker. In a country carrying one of the world's heaviest tuberculosis burdens, a chronic cough with fever and weight loss is treated as TB first. That reflex is often fatal, because B. pseudomallei is intrinsically resistant to many standard antibiotics, including the drugs used against TB.

The laboratory is the second weak link. Confirmation requires growing the bacterium in culture, yet automated identification systems used in most Indian labs frequently misread it as a relative — Burkholderia cepacia complex, Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter or Chromobacterium violaceum — or dismiss it as a contaminant. The selective medium that identifies it reliably, Ashdown's medium, is rarely stocked. Clinicians say a doctor must suspect melioidosis and tell the laboratory to look for it; without that instruction, the diagnosis is usually lost.

Who It Strikes

The infection is picked up through cuts in the skin, by inhaling contaminated dust or water droplets, or by drinking untreated water, and it peaks during and after the monsoon, when soil and surface water are churned up. Diabetes — particularly when poorly controlled — is the dominant risk factor, followed by chronic kidney and liver disease, heavy alcohol use, sickle cell disease and immune suppression. Farmers, fishermen, gardeners and construction workers who work barefoot or barehanded in wet soil face the most exposure.

That risk profile maps closely onto the parents and grandparents of the diaspora: older, often diabetic, living in precisely the coastal and agricultural districts where the bacterium thrives. A family in New Jersey or Toronto typically hears only that a parent has "TB" or "a chest infection" that is not responding. The useful question to ask the treating team is narrow and specific: has a blood or pus culture been done, and was the laboratory alerted to test for B. pseudomallei? The US CDC's clinical overview of melioidosis sets out the symptoms and the two-phase treatment in plain terms and is worth sharing with family and doctors alike.

Treatable, If Caught

Melioidosis is not a death sentence when it is named in time. Treatment runs in two phases: at least two weeks of intravenous ceftazidime or meropenem, then three to six months of oral co-trimoxazole to eradicate the bacterium and prevent relapse. The 48-year-old in Bhubaneswar recovered once the right drug replaced the wrong ones. What kills, doctors say, is the delay — weeks of TB therapy or broad-spectrum antibiotics while the infection spreads.

What Needs to Change

Specialists quoted by The Hindu — among them George Varghese of Christian Medical College, Vellore, and Rajeev Soman of Jupiter Hospital, Pune — point to the same fixes: make the disease notifiable so cases are counted, train peripheral laboratories to recognise the bacterium, stock selective media, and run public advisories during the monsoon, when exposure peaks. A cluster of deaths investigated last year in Turakapalem in Andhra Pradesh's Guntur district, initially of unknown cause, underlined how little surveillance exists outside major teaching hospitals. Until notification and laboratory capacity arrive, the study's 8.9% figure stands as the clearest warning available: in the wards where doctors looked properly, roughly one high-risk patient in eleven had an infection that routine practice would have missed.
